1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 14: Big Data and Data Science — our final chapter. This is Chapter 14 of the DMBOK, and at about two percent of the exam, it's one of the lighter chapters by weight. But it's also the most forward-looking, covering the technologies and techniques that are reshaping our field — data lakes, Hadoop, machine learning. There are a handful of precise facts the exam likes here, so let's learn them, and then celebrate finishing the course.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's our final plan. You'll define Big Data and the famous Vs, from Laney's original three to the expanded six. You'll explain the Lambda architecture and the data lake. You'll describe Hadoop, HDFS, and MapReduce. You'll distinguish the three types of machine learning. You'll recognize PMML, the NoSQL types, and the privacy concept of Datensparsamkeit. And you'll understand how to avoid the dreaded data swamp through governance. Let's begin.

1.title: Definitions & Goals
1.text: Let's define our terms. Big Data refers to extremely large data sets, characterized by high volume, velocity, and variety, that simply cannot be managed with traditional data management tools. That last phrase is the key — what makes data "big" isn't just size, it's that it overwhelms conventional tools. Data science is the interdisciplinary field that combines statistics, mathematics, programming, and crucially, domain knowledge, to extract insights from that data. There are three goals: enable analytics on large, diverse data sets beyond traditional tools; derive competitive insights from new data sources like social media, IoT, and logs; and support data science and machine learning initiatives. Remember: Big Data is data too big, too fast, or too varied for traditional tools.

1.title: The Vs of Big Data
1.text: The classic way to characterize Big Data is through the Vs, arranged around the hub on screen. Doug Laney of the META Group introduced the original three Vs back in 2001 — and that date and attribution are testable. The three are volume, the sheer scale of data measured in terabytes, petabytes, even exabytes; velocity, the speed at which data is generated and must be processed; and variety, the different types and formats, from structured to semi-structured to unstructured. Over time the model expanded to six Vs, adding veracity, the accuracy and trustworthiness of the data; viscosity, the resistance to data flow and processing; and virality, the rate at which data spreads and is shared. So for the exam: Laney, 2001, gave us the original three Vs, and the expanded model has six.

1.title: Business Drivers
1.text: What's driving organizations toward Big Data? Social media, the Internet of Things, and machine-generated data are producing volumes that exceed traditional database capacity. There's competitive advantage to be found in the insights buried in large unstructured datasets. There's cost reduction, because Big Data platforms run on cheap commodity hardware rather than expensive proprietary data warehouse appliances. There's the need for real-time analytics and event-driven processing. And there's the demand to support machine learning and AI applications. The key economic shift to remember: Big Data trades expensive specialized appliances for inexpensive, distributed commodity hardware.

1.title: Lambda Architecture (and CAP)
1.text: The classic Big Data processing architecture is the Lambda architecture, and notice it directly applies the CAP theorem we learned back in Chapter 6. It has three layers. The speed layer provides real-time views and, in CAP terms, favors availability and partition tolerance. The batch layer provides comprehensive, accurate views and favors consistency and availability. And the serving layer merges the batch and speed views to respond to queries. There's also a newer alternative called the Kappa architecture, which simplifies things by treating all data as a stream and eliminating the separate batch layer entirely — useful when you only need real-time processing. So remember: in Lambda, the speed layer is availability plus partition tolerance, the batch layer is consistency plus availability, and the serving layer merges them; Kappa is streaming-only.

1.title: The Data Lake
1.text: The data lake is one of the most important concepts in this chapter. A data lake is a repository that stores raw data in its native format until it's needed, using schema-on-read — meaning the structure is applied when you read the data, not when you write it. Contrast that with a data warehouse, which uses schema-on-write. Let's line them up, exactly as the side-by-side comparison on screen shows: the lake uses schema-on-read while the warehouse uses schema-on-write; the lake holds raw, unprocessed data while the warehouse holds processed, integrated data; the lake serves data scientists while the warehouse serves business analysts; and the lake uses ELT while the warehouse uses ETL. There's also a newer hybrid called the lakehouse, which combines the lake's low-cost, flexible storage with the warehouse's ACID transactions and schema enforcement on a single platform. The headline contrast: lake is schema-on-read, ELT, and raw; warehouse is schema-on-write, ETL, and processed.

1.title: Hadoop, HDFS & MapReduce
1.text: Hadoop is the foundational open-source framework for Big Data — a distributed computing framework that runs on commodity hardware, is designed to fail gracefully, and stores multiple copies of data for resilience. Two key components: HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System, which handles the distributed storage; and its use of MPP shared-nothing architecture — Massively Parallel Processing where each node is completely independent, with no shared memory or disk, which is what lets it scale across cheap hardware. The processing paradigm is MapReduce, which has three steps. Map distributes the data and the task across the nodes and processes them in parallel. Shuffle and sort groups and sorts the intermediate results. And reduce aggregates and combines those results into the final output. So memorize the MapReduce sequence: Map, then Shuffle and Sort, then Reduce — and remember Hadoop uses shared-nothing MPP.

1.title: Spark, ELT & Streaming
1.text: A few modern technologies that build on Hadoop. Apache Spark works like MapReduce but with one defining difference: it stores its intermediate processing results in memory, in RAM, rather than writing them to disk between steps. That dramatically reduces disk I/O and makes Spark far faster than MapReduce for iterative workloads like machine learning. Apache Kafka is a streaming platform — a distributed, durable, append-only log that lets multiple independent consumers read the same event stream, each at their own pace. And in Big Data environments, the preferred pattern is ELT — you load the raw data into the lake first, then transform it within Hadoop or Spark, letting the powerful target system do the processing work. Two facts to anchor: Spark is in-memory, and ELT loads first.

1.title: Machine Learning — 3 Types
1.text: Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence that gives computers the ability to learn from data without being explicitly programmed. There are three main types — the three cards on screen — and the exam tests the distinction. Supervised learning uses training data that includes labeled inputs and outputs, so the algorithm learns the mapping from input to output — examples are spam detection and credit scoring. Unsupervised learning uses data with no labels, so the algorithm finds patterns or structure on its own — examples are customer segmentation and anomaly detection. And reinforcement learning has an agent that learns by receiving rewards or penalties for its actions — think game-playing AI and robotics. The quick test: supervised means labeled data, unsupervised means unlabeled pattern-finding, and reinforcement means learning from rewards.

1.title: Algorithms, PMML & Responsible AI
1.text: A quick tour of the algorithms and standards. Common algorithms include regression for predicting continuous values, classification for assigning categories, clustering for grouping similar items in an unsupervised way, decision trees and random forests for rule-based classification, and neural networks for deep learning and pattern recognition. PMML, the Predictive Model Markup Language, is an XML-based standard for representing predictive models, and its key benefit is enabling model portability between different tools — so you can build a model in one tool and deploy it in another. Apache Mahout is an open-source machine learning library for Hadoop. And on responsible AI, model explainability is increasingly important because regulators, auditors, and the individuals affected by automated decisions may require understandable justifications for those decisions. Remember: PMML equals XML model portability, and explainability supports accountability and compliance.

1.title: NLP, NoSQL & BASE
1.text: A few more Big Data technologies. Natural Language Processing, NLP, is the field of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Two NLP applications worth knowing: sentiment analysis, which determines the emotional tone of text — positive, negative, or neutral — used for social media monitoring; and text mining, which extracts structured information from unstructured text. On the database side, the NoSQL types — which we met in Chapter 6 — include key-value stores for caching, document stores for JSON data, column-family stores for analytical and sparse data, and graph databases for relationship networks. And NoSQL databases follow the BASE properties: Basically Available, Soft State, and Eventual Consistency. The exam favorite here: graph databases excel at traversing highly connected data, like fraud rings and social networks.

1.title: Data Science Activities (7)
1.text: The DMBOK lays out seven data science activities. One, define the Big Data strategy and business needs. Two, choose your data sources, both internal and external. Three, acquire and ingest the data, through either streaming or batch ingestion — and importantly, apply metadata tags during ingestion. Four, develop the data science models, through exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, training, and validation. Five, deploy and monitor the models — often using PMML — and watch for model drift, where performance degrades over time. Six, publish the insights through visualization and storytelling. And seven, monitor the Big Data environment itself. Two practical exam points: apply metadata tags at ingestion, and watch for model drift after deployment.

1.title: Privacy, Visualization & Governance
1.text: Let's cover privacy, visualization, and governance together. There's a wonderful German term the exam likes: Datensparsamkeit, which means data minimization — the principle of collecting only the data that's strictly necessary for the stated purpose. It's foundational to GDPR and privacy-by-design, and it pushes back against Big Data's natural tendency to collect everything "just in case." For visualization, the key tools are R, the open-source statistical programming language; Python; and BI tools like Tableau and Power BI. And on governance, here's the crucial concept: without governance and metadata tagging, a data lake degrades into a data swamp — an unusable mess where data can't be found or trusted. Metadata tags applied at ingestion identify PII, data domains, and quality issues, enabling governance even without a predefined schema. So: Datensparsamkeit is data minimization, and a lack of governance turns a lake into a swamp.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate the final chapter's facts. The three Vs came from Doug Laney at META Group in 2001 — volume, velocity, variety — expanded to six with veracity, viscosity, and virality. The Lambda architecture has speed, batch, and serving layers, and Kappa is streaming-only. A data lake uses schema-on-read, ELT, and raw data. MapReduce goes Map, Shuffle and Sort, Reduce. Hadoop uses shared-nothing MPP and HDFS, while Spark is in-memory. The machine learning types are supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement. PMML provides XML model portability. Datensparsamkeit is data minimization. And an ungoverned data lake becomes a data swamp. That's your cheat sheet.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: The final chapter's traps. First, Laney's original contribution in 2001 was three Vs, not four — the others came later. Second, a data lake uses schema-on-read with ELT, not schema-on-write; that's the warehouse. Third, supervised learning uses labeled data, while unsupervised uses unlabeled data — don't reverse them. Fourth, Spark is in-memory, which is exactly what distinguishes it from disk-based MapReduce. And fifth, Big Data doesn't require proprietary appliances; it deliberately uses commodity, shared-nothing hardware. The signature phrases that point to right answers here are schema-on-read, in-memory, and data minimization.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's summarize Chapter 14. Big Data is data too voluminous, too fast, and too varied for traditional tools — captured by Laney's three Vs from 2001, expanded to six. The core architectures are Lambda, with its speed, batch, and serving layers built on CAP, and the data lake, with schema-on-read and ELT — and remember, an ungoverned lake becomes a swamp. Hadoop, using shared-nothing MPP and HDFS, runs MapReduce, and Spark is the faster in-memory successor. Machine learning comes in supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement varieties, and PMML gives you model portability. And Datensparsamkeit — data minimization — keeps Big Data ethical and compliant. That completes the chapter.

1.title: 🎓 Course Wrap-Up — You've Covered It All
1.text: And with that, congratulations — you've completed all fourteen chapters of the DMBOK Second Edition! Take a moment to appreciate how far you've come. You now hold the complete picture of data management: Data Governance sitting at the center of the DAMA Wheel, directing the eleven knowledge areas around it. You've mastered the big-weight four — Governance, Data Modeling, Metadata, and Data Quality — which together make up about forty-four percent of the exam, plus Reference and Master Data and Data Warehousing and BI for another twenty percent. Here's what to do next. Revisit the cheat-sheet slides in each module until the numbers and lists are automatic. Take full-length practice exams under timed conditions. And tab and bookmark your DMBOK for the open-book portion of the exam. One last piece of advice: aim for seventy percent or higher, which keeps the Practitioner and Master paths open for your future. You've put in the work — now go pass that exam. You've got this.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time for the final set of five practice questions, on Big Data and data science. These focus on the architecture distinctions — Spark versus MapReduce, Lambda versus Kappa — and on machine learning governance. Read each carefully, choose your answer, and then reveal the solution. Here we go, one last time.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: what most distinguishes Apache Spark from Hadoop MapReduce? The answer is C — Spark stores intermediate results in memory, in RAM, dramatically reducing disk I/O for iterative workloads. That in-memory processing is its defining advantage. The other statements are simply inaccurate.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: when are graph databases most advantageous over relational databases? The answer is D — when you need to traverse highly connected data to discover relationships, like fraud networks or social connections. Graph databases use index-free adjacency to follow relationships efficiently. Relational databases handle the other scenarios just fine.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: an organization processes only real-time streaming data and finds the batch layer adds needless complexity. Which architecture simplifies it? The answer is B — Kappa architecture, which treats all data as a stream and eliminates the separate batch layer. Lambda keeps the batch layer; data mesh and medallion address entirely different concerns. Two more on the final slide.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: which governance challenge is most commonly cited as data science teams scale? The answer is A — a lack of standardized processes for model versioning, reproducibility, and accountability for model outputs. Without these, you can't trust, audit, or reproduce your models. The other options describe implausible "problems," like too much documentation or too much labeled data. Question five: why is model explainability important in responsible AI? The answer is A — because regulators, auditors, and affected individuals may require understandable justifications for decisions made by or with machine learning models. Explainability is central to accountability and compliance. It does not replace bias assessments, it's not limited to unsupervised learning, and explainable models don't automatically outperform black-box models on accuracy. And that is the final question of the course. You've now worked through every knowledge area and every chapter the CDMP Fundamentals exam covers. Congratulations on completing the course — go review those cheat sheets, take your practice exams, and walk into that exam with confidence. I wish you the very best. You've got this.
